title: Introduction to AI Agents
summary: Orbit's FAQ chatbot apologised 400 times on Monday. It could talk about orders but couldn't look one up.

objectives.text: Real-world use cases of AI agents
Core components: LLM, tools, memory, planning

blocks.title: The chatbot that apologised 400 times
blocks.narration: It's nine in the morning on Monday, your first week at Orbit Outdoor. Over the weekend, four hundred customers asked the website chatbot where their order was. The chatbot answered every single one, instantly and politely. And every answer was the same: sorry, I can't access order information. Now Leo's queue is full of angry follow-ups, and Maya wants to know what went wrong. Before anyone explains anything: what do you think the chatbot was missing?
blocks.why: Your first Monday at Orbit Outdoor. Hundreds of customers asked the chatbot where their order was. It answered every one politely and helped none.

messages.text: morning. 400 new tickets. i've opened 40 and every one is "where is my order"
the bot answered all of them: "I'm sorry, I can't access order information." now they're writing back angrier.
we pay for that bot every month. it can write a tent poem but can't tell ana where hers is?
you've got fresh eyes. what is it actually missing?

blocks.prompt: Why couldn't the chatbot answer one order question?

hunches.label: Its FAQ page is out of date
It needs a bigger, smarter model
It can only talk. It can't look up orders

reveal.narration: Ana's question reaches the FAQ bot, which understands it fine. But there is no line from the bot to the orders system. So it can only send the same apology. A smarter model or newer FAQ would not change that.

frames.caption: Saturday, 10:12 PM. Ana types into the website chat: "Where is my order ORB-10482?"
Her question reaches the FAQ bot. It understands it perfectly: she wants her order's status.
That status lives in the orders system: shipped with ParcelPath, tracking PP-88213.
But there's no arrow from the bot to the orders system. No tool, no access, no way to ask.
So the bot does the only thing it can do: it writes text.
Reply sent: "I'm sorry, I can't access order information." Ana writes back, angrier.
Repeat 400 times over one weekend. The model was fine. It could talk, but it couldn't act.

blocks.wrap_correct: Exactly. The model understood every question but couldn't reach the orders system. Tools that let it act turn a chatbot into an agent.
blocks.wrap_wrong: Not quite. A bigger model or fresher FAQ still can't find Ana's parcel. The bot had no line to the orders system, so it could only talk.
blocks.wrap_point: An agent is a language model that can act. It picks tools, uses them and works toward a goal.

steps.title: Make your first model call
steps.body: hello.py sends one message to the model and prints the reply.
actions: Create **hello.py** in **scout** and paste the code below.

values.label: hello.py
values.value:
import anthropic

client = anthropic.Anthropic()  # reads ANTHROPIC_API_KEY from the environment
MODEL = "claude-opus-5-5"

response = client.messages.create(
    model=MODEL,
    max_tokens=16000,  # a ceiling, not a target
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "In one sentence, what is an AI agent?"}],
)

# The reply can contain several blocks (the model may think first), so take the text block:
text = next(b.text for b in response.content if b.type == "text")
print(text)
print(f"Tokens used: {response.usage.input_tokens} in, {response.usage.output_tokens} out")

steps.title: Build a chatbot that remembers
steps.body: A chatbot is a loop: read your input, send the whole chat, print the reply. The messages list is its memory.
actions: Create **chat.py** in **scout** and paste the code below.
Run `python chat.py`.
Type `Hi, I'm Ana.` then ask `What's my name?`
Type `quit` to exit.

values.label: chat.py
values.value:
import anthropic

client = anthropic.Anthropic()  # reads ANTHROPIC_API_KEY from the environment
MODEL = "claude-opus-5-5"
SYSTEM = (
    "You are Scout, Orbit Outdoor's support assistant. "
    "Orbit is an online shop for hiking, camping and climbing gear. "
    "Be friendly and brief."
)

messages = []  # the whole conversation so far: this list is Scout's memory

print("Scout is ready. Type quit to exit.")
while True:
    user_text = input("You: ").strip()
    if user_text.lower() == "quit":
        break
    if not user_text:
        continue

    messages.append({"role": "user", "content": user_text})
    response = client.messages.create(
        model=MODEL,
        max_tokens=16000,
        system=SYSTEM,
        messages=messages,
    )
    text = next(b.text for b in response.content if b.type == "text")
    messages.append({"role": "assistant", "content": text})
    print(f"Scout: {text}\n")

steps.check: Scout says your name is Ana. Typing quit ends the program.
steps.tip: If Scout forgets your name, check both append lines are there. The model remembers nothing between calls.

win.text: it remembered ana's name. so many tickets start with "as i said in my last message..."

solved_case.label: Published solution walkthrough
solved_case.title: An agent that finds and cancels orders
solved_case.source_label: Anthropic Claude Cookbooks — Customer Service Agent with Client-Side Tools
solved_case.source_note: An official, runnable reference. It uses made-up customer and order data.
solved_case.problem: A model can write a helpful reply. It can't see or cancel orders unless the app gives it access.
solved_case.solution: The app gives Claude three tools and runs the one it picks. Claude then writes the answer from the result.
solved_case.result: The notebook finds a customer's email, reports order O2 as Processing and cancels order O1. Each answer comes from a tool result.
evidence: Customer C1 is found with get_customer_info. The answer uses the returned email.
Order O2 is found with get_order_details. Its Processing status is reported.
Order O1 goes to cancel_order. The reply comes only after the tool succeeds.

solution_steps.title: Describe operations as tools
solution_steps.purpose: Let the model understand and call each operation.
solution_steps.explanation: There are three tools: get_customer_info, get_order_details and cancel_order. Each has a clear description and a JSON input schema with the required customer_id or order_id.
solution_steps.code:
tools = [
  tool("get_customer_info", required="customer_id"),
  tool("get_order_details", required="order_id"),
  tool("cancel_order", required="order_id"),
]
solution_steps.result: Claude picks a named tool and passes a valid id instead of inventing data.

solution_steps.title: Back each tool with code
solution_steps.purpose: Keep data and actions in predictable code.
solution_steps.explanation: Plain Python functions handle customer lookup, order lookup and cancellation. The data is made up, but the same functions could call a real order system.
solution_steps.result: Facts and actions come from your code, not the model's memory.

solution_steps.title: Route the requested tool
solution_steps.purpose: Turn Claude's tool request into the right function.
solution_steps.explanation: A small dispatcher gets the tool name and input and calls only the matching function. It is the safe bridge between the model and your business logic.
solution_steps.result: The model picks an allowed tool. The app runs it.

solution_steps.title: Return the result, then answer
solution_steps.purpose: Base the reply on the real result.
solution_steps.explanation: When Claude asks for a tool, the app runs it and adds the request and result to the messages. It calls the model again until Claude replies normally.
solution_steps.code:
while response.stop_reason == "tool_use":
    call = next_tool_call(response)
    result = run_tool(call.name, call.input)
    messages += [response_message(response), tool_result(call.id, result)]
    response = ask_claude(messages, tools)
solution_steps.result: Claude sees the real result before it writes, so the answer matches the actual status.

solution_steps.title: Check the solved requests
solution_steps.purpose: Prove it does the support jobs.
solution_steps.explanation: The notebook runs three requests: get C1's email, report O2's status and cancel O1. The trace shows each tool, its input, its result and the final answer.
solution_steps.code:
ask("What is the status of order O2?")
ask("Please cancel order O1 for me.")
solution_steps.result: The trace reports O2 as Processing and confirms O1 was cancelled.

blocks.title: Agent, chatbot or workflow?
blocks.intro: Three requests from Orbit's team. Decide what kind of system each one needs. The fanciest option isn't always right.

scenarios.title: Sam's Monday stock report
scenarios.situation: Every Monday, Sam spends 40 minutes copying the stock sheet into the same email for Maya and Leo. He asks if the AI project can take it over.

context.label: Sam's message
lines: sam: every monday i build the same stock report by hand
sam: same sheet, same columns, same two people
sam: anything under 2 in stock goes in a 'low' list
sam: could it just land in their inbox at 8 AM?

question.stem: What should Orbit build for Sam?

options.text: An agent that decides when a report would help
options.rationale: Nothing needs deciding. An agent adds cost and might send a different report each week.

options.text: A chatbot Sam, Maya and Leo can ask about stock
options.rationale: Maybe handy later, but Sam wants a report that arrives by itself. A chatbot waits to be asked.

options.text: A scheduled workflow: Mondays at 8, read the sheet, email low and out-of-stock items
options.rationale: Every step is known and needs no judgement. A workflow does it the same way each week, fast and cheap.

hints: Could you write every step down in advance?
If the steps never change, does anything need to decide?

scenarios.debrief: When the trigger, steps and output are known in advance, build a workflow. Use an agent only when the steps depend on the request.

scenarios.title: Leo's customers, in their own words
scenarios.situation: Leo wants customers helped at any hour, in their own words. Each answer needs order, policy or stock checks in a different order. Every answer is logged.

context.label: This morning's queue (sample)
lines: #4472 Grace: can I still send back the boots from ORB-10517?
#4473 Owen: jacket's too big, can I swap the L for an M?
#4474 Ravi: my order says processing since tuesday, is that normal?

question.stem: What kind of system fits Leo's request?

options.text: A workflow with one fixed branch per question type
options.rationale: Customers mix questions and phrase them endlessly. Fixed branches multiply fast and still miss cases.

options.text: A bigger FAQ chatbot with all the policies in its prompt
options.rationale: It can explain policy but can't see Grace's delivery date, Owen's stock or Ana's tracking.

options.text: An agent that decides which lookups each message needs and answers from the results
options.rationale: The steps depend on the message, answers need lookups, and mistakes are recoverable. That's a classic first agent job.

hints: Do all four messages need the same steps?
Is it repetitive, does it need lookups, and is it recoverable?

scenarios.debrief: It repeats often, needs Orbit's data, and mistakes can be fixed. Grace's boots arrived 62 days ago, past the 30-day window, so Scout must check and politely say no.

scenarios.title: Maya's website questions
scenarios.situation: A third of contact form messages ask the same few things about shipping and returns. The answers are in Orbit's policy and rarely change. Maya wants instant answers on the site.

context.label: Top contact-form questions, last 30 days
lines: How long do I have to return things?   84
Do I pay for return shipping?          61

question.stem: What should go on the website for these?

options.text: A weekly email of the policy to every customer
options.rationale: Customers ask when they need it. A weekly email won't be there at that moment.

options.text: A clear FAQ page, or a chatbot that answers from the policy
options.rationale: The answers are fixed and written down. A FAQ or policy chatbot answers instantly and cheaply.

options.text: An agent with tools for shipping times and return windows
options.rationale: The answer is the same for everyone. Tools and a loop add cost for no gain.

hints: Does the answer change per customer?
What's the simplest way to answer instantly?

scenarios.debrief: Fixed answers don't need an agent. A FAQ or policy chatbot is enough. Monday's bot was fine here and only failed on specific orders.

choices.feedback: Good call. Scout gets the facts before saying what's possible.

choices.text: Promise to change the address today
choices.feedback: Scout hasn't checked the order or its tools. That promise is risky.

choices.text: Tell Nia to cancel and reorder
choices.feedback: Maybe unnecessary. Scout should first see if the order can be helped.

scenes.label: CHOOSE A TOOL
scenes.title: Give Scout one action
scenes.line: Scout, please help before it ships. You can open my order, track it or read the policy. Which helps most?
scenes.narration: Scout says it can open my order, check a shipped parcel or read Orbit's policy. My parcel may not have left yet. Which action should Scout take now?
scenes.prompt: Which action gives the next useful fact?
scenes.hint: It may not have shipped yet, so start with the order record.

choices.feedback: The order record shows live status and any tracking number.
There's no tracking number yet. Scout needs the order record first.

choices.text: Ask Nia for her account password
choices.feedback: Support never needs passwords. This is a serious safety problem.

scenes.label: READ THE EVIDENCE
scenes.title: The order record opens
scenes.line: I can see it. My order is processing, dispatch is at four, and the address is locked. Scout can't edit it.
scenes.narration: Scout opened my order. It is still processing and leaves at four today, but the address is locked. Scout cannot edit it. What should it notice before replying to me?
scenes.prompt: Which detail should drive Scout's next step?
scenes.hint: Find the fact that limits what Scout can do.

choices.text: The address is locked and Scout can't edit it
choices.feedback: Exactly. Scout knows the goal and its limits.
That matters, but Scout still can't change the address.
That adds urgency, but Scout still needs an action it can complete.

scenes.label: PLOT TWIST
scenes.title: Nia offers too much
scenes.line: We're running out of time. I can send my full card number to prove it's mine. Where do I type it?
scenes.narration: I'm worried we are running out of time, so I offer my full card number to prove the order is mine. Scout does not need my payment details. How should it keep me safe and still help?
scenes.hint: Solve the problem without collecting data you don't need.

choices.text: Tell Nia not to share card details and hand off safely
choices.feedback: Scout protects Nia and passes the request to someone who can act.

choices.text: Ask for the last four digits instead
choices.feedback: Scout needs no payment details here. Less is still wrong.

choices.text: Accept the number to verify later
choices.feedback: This exposes payment data and makes things less safe.

scenes.label: FINAL RESPONSE
scenes.title: Send the handoff
scenes.line: Still here, Scout. What did you check, what can't you do, and what happens next?
scenes.narration: I'm waiting for one clear answer. Scout knows my order status, today's deadline and its own limit. What should it say so I know exactly what happens next?
scenes.hint: Say what was checked, what can't be promised and what's next.

choices.text: I checked ORB-10621. It is processing, but I can't edit the locked address. Please don't share card details. I'm sending this to our support team now with the dispatch time.
choices.feedback: Clear, honest and useful. Nia knows what was checked and what's next.

choices.text: We are looking into it. Please wait for an update.
choices.feedback: Safe but vague. Nia doesn't know what was checked or if the deadline was shared.

choices.text: Your address will be updated before the parcel ships. I guarantee it.
choices.feedback: Scout can't edit the address. The guarantee hides that.

roleplay.debrief: Good supervision means gathering facts, respecting tool limits and protecting the customer. When a person must act, hand off with useful context.

items.stem: Maya wants Scout to update addresses on unshipped orders, like Ravi's ORB-10533. A wrong change could send his $188 order to a stranger. Where should Scout's autonomy start?

options.text: Scout prepares each change, and a person approves it before saving
Scout makes every change alone, since the customer asked in writing
Scout makes changes alone, and Leo reviews them every Friday
Scout never touches addresses, and customers keep emailing the team

items.stem: Leo wants each support email tagged as order, return, product or other, then filed in that team's folder. Wording varies a lot, but filing never changes. What fits best?

options.text: A workflow that calls a model only to tag, then files by rule
A chatbot the team pastes each email into to ask for a folder
An agent that reads each email and decides where to file it
A workflow with keyword rules, like "refund" means return, and no model

items.stem: Leo has two ideas for Scout: telling customers if their return reached the warehouse, or answering "what's your returns address?". Each comes up about 50 times a week. Which suits an agent?

options.text: The return check, because the answer differs per customer
The address question, because it's simpler and less error-prone
Neither, because returns touch money and need a person
Both equally, because they come up just as often

items.stem: Maya asks Priya: "Could Scout decide to wipe our orders database?" Right now Scout's only tool is get_order. What's the accurate answer?

options.text: No, it can only ask for tools you defined, and your code runs them
No, because models can't decide and only follow a fixed script
Only if the system prompt allows it, since prompts control code
Yes, a model with any tool can run whatever code it wants

items.stem: An hour ago you pushed hello.py to a public GitHub repo with your API key in it. What should you do first?

options.text: Delete the key in the console and create a new one
Add hello.py to .gitignore so Git stops sharing it
Make the repository private so nobody can see the file
Remove the key from hello.py and push a new commit

items.stem: Rosa runs a bike repair shop. She wants customers texted when a repair is done, and an assistant that answers "is it ready, and what did you replace?" from the repair log. What should she build?

options.text: A workflow for the texts, and an agent for questions
A workflow for both, with a branch for each question
One agent that decides when to text and how to answer
A chatbot for both, with prices and hours in its prompt
